headline: Given each library its hand-written best practice, the field converges on `vanilla` — which is the finding: parity with next-yak's automatic custom-property split costs a manual class-plus-inline-style split in every component that has a dynamic value.

microbench.why: Each lane here gets the hand-written workaround its docs recommend: a static class plus the per-instance value on an inline `style`. That is what next-yak's compiler emits by itself, and the field converges on it — `vanilla` 0.604 ms/1k, the css-prop fold 0.617, `bamboo` 0.634, `cnfast` 0.640, `tailwind-merge` 0.651. `styled-components` climbs from 4.51 ms/1k in the naive Example `dyn-translate` to 1.35 here and `goober` from 5.98 to 1.06, because `.attrs` and a hoisted class stop the per-value hash from running. The parity is real; what the chart cannot show is that a developer writes that split by hand, per component, for every dynamic value, while next-yak ships the same transform as a feature.

autocannon.why: The css-prop fold serves 1285 req/s and `vanilla` 1188, with `cnfast` (1158), `tailwind-merge` (1143) and `bamboo` (1138) inside 4% of it. `styled-components` recovers from 206 req/s in the naive case to 622 here and `goober` from 158 to 757. `panda` stays at 280, since its `css()` call still resolves per element even with the value moved to an inline style.

attribution.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` renders in 0.747 ms with a 0.211 ms library slice and `vanilla` in 0.791. `styled-components` drops to 1.02 ms of library time from 4.40 in the naive case, `.attrs` writing an inline style instead of deriving a class, and `goober` to 0.551 from 6.02. `bamboo` reports no library slice at all and costs 1.07 ms, the same react-dom class-bytes tax it pays everywhere else. `panda` is the exception at 3.96 ms, still resolving its object per element.

hydrate.why: Every lane hydrates as pure JS once the value rides an inline style: 49.2-52.8 ms across the extracted and atomic builds, with no style or layout in the span. `styled-components` improves to 90.5 ms from 117 in the naive case and `goober` to 89.0 from 1330. `emotion` at 77.1 ms still serializes its static rule on the client.

inp.why: Moving one dot costs 0.39-0.96 ms of JS in every lane, and the bars sit between 6.5 and 8.2 ms for all but three: `emotion` 10.7 ms, `panda` 14.1 and `panda-props` 22.0, each re-resolving its object on the interaction. The hand-written split removes the rest of the field's reason to differ.

mount.why: Cold mount lands at 65.9-71.3 ms for the extracted, atomic and utility lanes, `bamboo` at 67.8 among them. `goober` mounts in 86.1 ms against 1320 in the naive case, the clearest single measurement of what the hand-written split buys. `emotion` (96.9 ms) and `panda` (84.7 ms) trail.

renderTiming.why: One recalculation and one layout everywhere, the recalc costing 0.102-0.189 ms. A single static rule plus an inline style gives the browser one class to match however many instances there are.

payload.why: The css-prop fold ships 5.24 kB gzipped and `vanilla` 5.50. The hand-written split is worth 20-30 kB to the runtime lanes: `emotion` drops from 39.3 kB in the naive case to 18.3 here and `styled-components` from 35.3 to 18.9, since the sheet no longer carries a rule per instance. `bamboo` ships 7.46 kB and `panda` 9.34.

nsweep.why: At 4000 dots `vanilla` holds 2.67 ms, the css-prop fold 2.71, `cnfast` 2.73 and `bamboo` 2.87, all with one rule regardless of n. `styled-components` reaches 5.66 ms against 19.7 in the naive case and `goober` 4.60 against 164. `panda` at 12.2 ms is the only shipped lane that still scales its own work with n.

crossCase: `dyn-fair` is the hand-optimized middle of the dynamic trio (the Example `dyn-translate` above is the naive version, `dyn-inline` below the pure inline-style control). Every library reaches near-`vanilla` here only because the developer manually splits the static class from the dynamic value, writing by hand what next-yak's custom-property compile does automatically: next-yak's own figures barely move between the two cases (1.18 to 1.23 ms/1k) because there was nothing to change. The parity is real and so is its price, the same optimization repeated per component, per dynamic value, forever, and `dyn-translate` shows what the code costs when nobody pays it.
